how-much-can-i-raise-storage-rent.html.text:
SELF-STORAGE RATE MANAGEMENT

How much can I raise rent on an existing storage tenant?

Operators ask this as a question about the percentage — 8%, 12%, 20% — and it is really a question about move-outs. Any increase is worth sending if it survives the churn it causes, and the reason so many are sent too small is that the churn is priced wrong: a departing tenant is counted at their rent, as though the unit sits empty for the rest of the year. It does not. It re-lets at your street rate, which on a long-tenured unit is usually above what the leaver was paying.

This page works one increase all the way through. The self-storage rate increase calculator does the same arithmetic on your own numbers, in your browser, with nothing uploaded.

Open the calculator

The example

A single facility, one cohort of 42 units of the same size, all at an in-place rent of $118 a month. The street rate for that size today is $149. Tenant protection and other per-unit income runs $12 a month on an occupied unit. When a unit turns over it sits empty 45 days, the replacement tenant gets the usual free first month, and the turn — clean-out, lock, listing, admin — costs $45. Over the next twelve months about 22% of this cohort would move out whatever you do.

The proposal is a 15% increase: $118 to $135.70, or $17.70 more per unit per month.

What a move-out actually costs

Start with the figure the decision is usually made on. A tenant paying the raised rent is worth $1,772 over twelve months once the $12 of ancillary income is counted. That is the number in an operator’s head when the increase letters go out, and it is not what a move-out costs.

What a move-out costs is that value minus what the unit earns after it is re-let, which comes to four terms:

TermAmount
Rent and ancillary lost over 45 days empty$238
Free first month for the replacement tenant$149
Turn: clean-out, lock, listing, admin$45
Re-rent at $149 street instead of their $135.70-$160
What one induced move-out costs$272

$272, not $1,772. The fourth line is the one that does the work and the one no rule of thumb carries: the replacement pays more than the person who left, for every month of the horizon, and that credit cancels most of the downtime. It is also the line that reverses when the raised rent goes above street, which is the single most important thing to know before deciding how far to push a long-tenured cohort.

So how much churn does the increase survive?

With a move-out costing $272 and every staying tenant paying $17.70 more for twelve months, the increase is worth $6,272 across the cohort over the horizon — and it would still be worth exactly nothing only if it drove out 60.8% of the group, or about 25 of the 42 units, on top of the 22% who were leaving anyway. If it caused no extra move-outs at all it would be worth $6,958, so even a heavy response takes a surprisingly small bite.

Put that next to what an operator would actually expect from a $17.70 increase — two or three units — and the decision stops being close. The value of the calculation is not that it says yes; it is that it converts an unanswerable question (how many will leave?) into an answerable one (would twenty-five of them leave?).

The same cohort at other increases

IncreaseNew rentBreak-even move-outsWorth over 12 months
5%$123.9042.2%$1,990
8%$127.4451.0%$3,274
10%$129.8054.8%$4,131
12%$132.1657.6%$4,987
15%$135.7060.8%$6,272
20%$141.6064.4%$8,413
25%$147.5066.7%$10,554

The last column holds the move-out response constant, which is the assumption to be suspicious of: a 25% increase does not provoke the same churn a 5% one does. That is why this table names no best row. What it does show is the shape of the trade — the tolerance for move-outs widens as the increase grows, because everyone who stays is paying more — and it shows where the cohort would cross its own street rate, which is where the arithmetic changes character rather than degree.

Common questions

How much can I raise rent on an existing storage tenant?

The honest answer is that the size of the increase is not what decides it — the cost of the move-outs it causes is, and that cost is far smaller than it looks whenever the unit re-rents above the leaver’s rent. On the worked example above, 42 units at $118 raised 15% to $135.70 against a $149 street rate, the increase is worth $6,272 over twelve months and would only stop paying if it drove 60.8% of the group out, on top of ordinary churn. That is 25 of 42 units. The number to argue about is not the 15%; it is whether you believe 25 people would leave over $17.70 a month.

Why is a move-out cheaper than the rent I lose?

Because the unit does not stay empty. Price a move-out at the departing tenant’s rent and you are assuming the space earns nothing for the rest of the year, which is only true if you never re-let it. What you actually give up is the gap between keeping them and re-letting: the rent lost during lease-up, the move-in concession the replacement gets, and the turn cost — minus the difference between your street rate and what the leaver was paying. On the example that comes to $272 rather than $1,772, and the last term is a credit of $160 rather than a cost.

What changes when the raised rent is above street?

The credit becomes a charge, and the arithmetic turns. Below street, losing a tenant hands you a unit you re-let for more than they were paying. Above street, you lose the tenant and re-let for less, so the same move-out costs the downtime, the concession, the turn and the rate difference. The break-even move-out rate falls accordingly, and it falls fastest exactly where operators are most tempted — on long-tenured tenants whose rents have been raised several times already.

Does a bigger increase always beat a smaller one?

Not in practice, and the table above is deliberately not a recommendation. Arithmetically a larger increase collects more from everyone who stays, so it can absorb a higher move-out rate: on this example 5% breaks even at 42.2% churn and 25% breaks even at 66.7%. What that table cannot know is how much churn each increase actually provokes, which is a fact about your tenants and your market, not about the arithmetic. Read each row as a question — would more than this share walk? — and stop at the last row you can answer yes to.

How do I measure the move-out rate my last increase caused?

Compare the group you raised against a group you did not, over the same window, from your own management software. Move-outs in the 60 to 90 days after a notice, minus the move-out rate of an unraised group of similar size and tenure, is the induced rate this calculator asks for. Two increases measured that way are worth more than any published benchmark, because tenure mix and local vacancy differ so widely between facilities that a national average tells you almost nothing about yours.

Is this legal or financial advice?

No. It is arithmetic on figures you supply. It makes no determination about what your lease or your state’s self-storage act permits, what notice a tenant is owed before an increase takes effect, or whether raising rent is right for your business. Verify every figure against your own records and a qualified professional before acting on it.

Run it on your own numbers

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, what notice your lease or your state’s self-storage act requires before an increase takes effect, or whether raising a tenant’s rent is a good idea. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, and the numbers on this page are an illustrative example rather than market data. Verify every figure against your own management software, your leases, and a qualified professional before acting on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator runs entirely on your device; your rents, street rates and unit counts are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count.

FOR INDEPENDENT SELF-STORAGE OPERATORS

A move-out costs the gap, not the rent.

Every existing-customer rate increase comes down to one number nobody has: how many move-outs it can cause before it stops paying for itself. The reason the guess runs low is that a lost tenant is priced at their rent — but the unit does not sit empty, it re-lets at your street rate, which is usually above what a long-tenured tenant is paying. Put a real group of units in below and see what a move-out actually costs, and the churn rate the increase would have to survive.

How much can I raise rent on an existing storage tenant? — the worked example in full

Compare: this calculator vs. SiteLink, or this calculator vs. pricing a move-out at the tenant's rent.

The units you are raising

One group of comparable units — same size, same in-place rent, same tenure band. Mixed sizes are separate runs; averaging them hides the cohort that should not be raised.

What you expect to happen

The second figure is the assumption the whole decision rests on, and no arithmetic can supply it. Enter what you believe; the panel tells you how wrong you could be and still come out ahead.

What a turnover costs you

Your own lease-up time and turn cost, from your management software. These three are what make a move-out expensive; the street rate above is what makes it cheap.

The same decision at other increases

The row in bold is what you entered. Read the break-even column as a question: do you believe more than that share of this group would leave over that much a month?

Fix the errors above and the table will fill in.

A bigger increase buys more from everyone who stays, so it can absorb more move-outs — but the response it provokes grows too, and this tool does not model that. It prices the decision; the churn is yours to judge.

      Common questions

      How many move-outs can a rate increase absorb?

      Far more than most operators assume, and this calculator gives the number rather than a feeling. On the worked example the page opens with — 42 units at $118, a 15% increase, a $149 street rate, 45 days to lease up and a free first month — the increase stays profitable until it causes a 60.8% induced move-out rate on top of ordinary churn. That is 25 of the 42 units, against the 2 or 3 an operator would actually expect. The reason the tolerance is so wide is that a vacated unit does not stay vacant: it re-rents at the street rate, which is above what a long-tenured tenant is paying.

      What does one move-out actually cost me?

      Not the rent. On the worked example a tenant who leaves costs $272, not the $1,772 of rent and tenant-protection income they would have paid over a year. The $272 is four terms: $238 of rent lost while the unit sits empty for 45 days, $149 for the free first month the replacement tenant gets, $45 to clean the unit and re-lock and re-list it, minus $160 because the replacement pays the $149 street rate rather than the $135.70 the leaver was raised to. That last term is the one nobody carries in their head, and it is negative — it makes the move-out cheaper — for every unit whose in-place rent sits below street.

      Should I raise an existing tenant above my street rate?

      It is the point at which the arithmetic turns against you, and the calculator flags it. Below street, a move-out is cheap because the unit comes back at more than the leaver was paying. Above street, the same move-out is expensive twice over: you lose the tenant and you re-let at less than they were paying, so the re-rent term flips from a credit to a cost and the break-even move-out rate falls sharply. There is also the part no arithmetic sees — a tenant who checks your website finds a cheaper unit at your own facility, which is the version of this decision that ends up on a review site.

      How often can I raise rent on existing tenants?

      That is a question for your lease and your state, not for this tool, and the answer varies: month-to-month storage leases typically permit an increase with written notice, and the required notice period, delivery method and any cap are set by the lease terms and by state self-storage statutes. This calculator makes no determination about what your lease permits or what notice you owe — it prices the increase you are considering, assuming you have confirmed you may make it. Check the lease and your state’s self-storage act, and ask a lawyer if the answer is not plainly written.

      What move-out rate should I expect from a 15% increase?

      Nobody can tell you that from outside your facility, and a tool that pretended to would be guessing with your revenue. Induced churn depends on tenure, unit size, what the competitor down the road is asking, how the letter is written and how much slack the local market has. What this calculator does is turn the guess into a threshold you can judge: instead of asking how many will leave, ask whether you believe more than 60.8% of this group would walk over $17.70 a month. That is a question an operator who has sent increase letters before can answer, and it is a much easier one.

      Does this work for a facility with mixed unit sizes?

      Run it once per group. The arithmetic is per-unit and the inputs are per-group, so a 10x10 cohort at $118 and a 5x5 cohort at $64 are two runs, not one — their street rates, lease-up times and tenant tenures differ, and averaging them hides exactly the cohort that should not be raised. A facility-wide answer is the sum of the group answers, and the groups that fail are the ones worth knowing about.

      What if a vacated unit does not re-rent?

      Then the increase stops being cheap, and it is the input that moves the answer most. Everything above assumes a vacated unit comes back — after 45 days, at street rate. In a soft market a share of them simply sit, and that share is a separate question from how long a lease-up takes. Set it and watch the break-even: on the worked example, dropping the re-rent share from 100% to 80% raises the cost of one move-out from $272 to $581 and cuts the break-even move-out rate from 60.8% to 28.5%. The turnover cost is still charged on every vacated unit, because you clean it out, re-lock it and list it whether or not anyone takes it. If you do not know your own figure, run it at 100% and again at your worst month and see whether the decision changes.

      Is any of this uploaded?

      No. There is no account and the page makes no network requests — it runs entirely in your browser. Your rents, your street rates, your unit counts and the answers worked out from them are never sent anywhere and never appear in a usage count. The optional counter records only which features were used and the day, stored on your own device, and it switches itself off for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

      Is this legal, tax, or financial advice?

      No. It is arithmetic on the figures you type. It makes no determination about what your lease or your state’s self-storage act permits, what notice a tenant is owed, what a unit is worth, or whether an increase is a good idea for your business. Verify every figure against your own management software, your lease, and a qualified professional before you send an increase letter from it.

It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, and the numbers it starts with are an illustrative example rather than market data. Verify every figure against your own management software, your leases, and a qualified professional before acting on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

vs-pricing-a-move-out-at-the-tenants-ren.text:
← Self-Storage Rate Increase Calculator

This calculator vs. pricing a move-out at the tenant's rent

“If six of them leave, that's $8,000 a year gone” is not a cost — it is a cost with the re-let uplift silently left out, quietly making every rate increase look riskier than it is.

What pricing a move-out at the tenant's rent is

It is the mental model behind almost every gut check on a rate increase: a tenant leaves, so the facility loses whatever that tenant was paying, multiplied by however long the unit might have stayed occupied. It is easy to do in your head, and it is the number that makes an increase feel risky enough to skip.

It is wrong because the unit does not sit empty for the horizon — it gets re-let, usually at the facility's own current street rate, which is often higher than what the departing tenant was paying at the old, unraised rent. Pricing the move-out at the rent counts the loss and never counts what comes back in behind it.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the proposed increase, the street rate, the vacancy before a unit re-lets, the move-in concession, the turnover cost, and your move-out assumptions. It nets the re-let at street rate against the vacancy, concession, and turnover, and returns the real cost of one induced move-out, the break-even move-out rate for the whole group, and the margin of safety in percentage points — for this increase, not a rule of thumb about rent lost.

What pricing a move-out at the rent doesWhat this calculator does instead
Counts the departing tenant's rent (or the new, raised rent) over the horizon as the whole cost of a move-out. Nets the re-let at your own street rate against that figure, so a move-out only costs what actually goes unrecovered.
Has no line for the vacancy between tenants, so a fast-turning unit and a slow one look the same. Prices the days empty before re-letting as its own line, so vacancy risk shows up rather than disappearing into a flat rent figure.
Folds the move-in concession and turnover cost into the same lump as the "lost" rent, or ignores them. Itemises the concession and turnover cost as their own lines, so each is visible instead of buried in a bigger, wrong number.
Implies a low break-even move-out rate, because every move-out looks nearly as expensive as keeping the tenant. Reports a break-even move-out rate against the real cost, which is usually far higher — more room to send the increase than the naive number suggests.
Gives no way to see how much the gap changes when street rate moves relative to the raised rent. Flags the case where the raised rent lands above your own street rate, which is exactly when the naive and real numbers converge and the risk becomes real.

One increase, two ways of costing a move-out

Using this calculator's own worked example: 42 units at $118, a 15% increase to $135.70, a $149 street rate, a 45-day vacancy, a one-month concession, and a $45 turnover cost, judged over 12 months.

Pricing a move-out at the new rent plus ancillary income over the horizon puts the cost at $1,772.40 per move-out. Against the $8,920.80 the increase is worth across the group if nobody leaves, that implies the increase only survives losing about 5.03 of the 42 units — 12.0% — before the higher rent's gain is wiped out.

Netting the re-let at the $149 street rate against the vacancy, concession, and turnover puts the real cost of one induced move-out at $272.43 — about a sixth of the naive figure, because most of what looks like lost rent comes back in with the next tenant at street rate. On the real number, this calculator puts the break-even move-out rate at 60.8% of the group — a margin of safety of 54.8 percentage points, roughly five times more room than the naive 12.0% break-even suggests.

Nobody is being careless by reaching for the naive number first — it is the number a rent roll makes easy to see. The gap is the re-let uplift, and it is invisible until the street rate is priced against the raised rent directly, which is what this calculator does and a mental "rent times tenants" estimate cannot.

Common questions

Why does pricing a move-out at the tenant's rent get a rate increase wrong?

Because the unit does not sit empty forever -- it gets re-let, usually at the facility's own street rate, which is often higher than what the departing tenant was paying. On this calculator's own worked example (42 units, $118 to $135.70, a 15% increase), pricing a move-out at the new rent over a 12-month horizon says it costs $1,772.40. Netting the re-let at street rate against the vacancy, the move-in concession, and the turnover cost puts the real figure at $272.43 -- about a sixth of the naive number, because most of what looks like lost rent comes back in with the next tenant.

How big is the gap in the break-even move-out rate?

On the same worked example, pricing a move-out at the tenant's rent implies the increase only survives losing about 12.0% of the group (5.03 of 42 units) before the higher rent's total gain is wiped out. Costing each move-out properly puts the break-even at 60.8% -- five times more room. An operator using the naive number would reject or shrink an increase that the real arithmetic says can absorb far more churn than any realistic response.

What does pricing a move-out at the tenant's rent leave out entirely?

The re-rent uplift: the difference between the street rate a new tenant pays and the raised rent the departing tenant would have paid. It also leaves out that the concession and turnover cost are real but comparatively small line items next to that uplift, so lumping everything into "the rent, gone" overstates the loss on every one of the four components it never separates.

Is pricing a move-out at the tenant's rent ever close enough?

When the street rate is at or below the raised rent -- a soft local market, or a facility that has not raised its own asking rate in a while -- the re-let uplift shrinks toward zero and the naive number gets closer to the real one. The risk is trusting that closeness without checking street rate against the raised rent for this specific group, because the gap widens fast once street pulls ahead.

Does this calculator know what to charge or what my move-out rate will be?

No. It has no data on your market, your tenants, or how they will respond to a letter. It takes your rent, street rate, vacancy, concession, turnover cost, and move-out assumptions, and turns them into a break-even move-out rate and a margin of safety for this specific increase -- the arithmetic pricing a move-out at the rent skips, not a forecast of what tenants will do.

Open the Self-Storage Rate Increase Calculator to price your own increase, or read how much you can raise storage rent.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice, and it does not tell you what to charge, what notice your lease or your state’s self-storage act requires before an increase takes effect, or whether raising a tenant’s rent is a good idea. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, and the numbers it starts with are an illustrative example rather than market data. Verify every figure against your own management software, your leases, and a qualified professional before acting on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

← Self-Storage Rate Increase Calculator

This calculator vs. SiteLink

Two different shapes: SiteLink is an account-based platform for running a self-storage facility's whole operation, including automated rate rules once an increase policy is set. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — is this specific rate increase worth the move-outs it will cause.

What each tool is for

SiteLink, sold by Storable, is a self-storage facility management platform used by operators from single-site owners to national multi-facility companies. It runs tenant records, online rentals, billing and payments, and a Price Optimizer feature that helps set street rates and automate existing-customer rate-increase rules, tied to one account used on an ongoing paid basis across the whole facility. SiteLink's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that revenue-management software describe setting and automating rate rules across a facility; none describe working out, for one proposed increase, how many move-outs it can absorb before it loses money — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what SiteLink does. It does not store tenant records, take online rentals, or automate a rule across a portfolio. It takes one proposed existing-customer rate increase — the tenants it applies to, the street rate, the move-in concession a replacement tenant gets, the turnover cost, and a horizon — and turns that into the induced move-out rate at which the increase breaks even, the units that represents, the margin of safety in percentage points, and what the increase is worth across the group at every step from 5% to 25%, with a flag on any rung that prices the raised rent above the facility's own street rate. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
